newsitem.title: UK: Sterling rally seen limited above 2.80 marks.
newsitem.headline: Sterling rally seen limited above 2.80 marks.

text.p: Sterling's dramatic recovery this week from troughs around 2.72 marks to above 2.79 marks by Friday was stoked as investors banked on higher rates, but analysts warn the upside may now be limited.
"We see a little more upside for sterling from here but I suspect we are not going to see a test of the old (2.8330-mark) highs," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
A raft of mixed economic data, including key unemployment and inflation numbers, failed to dampen the pound's rally as it came on the heels of a hawkish Bank of England report on inflation.

Only last week rates were hoisted to 6.25 percent from 6.0 in a bid to keep inflation in check. But the BoE on Tuesday, in its first report since it was granted freedom to set rates, warned inflation was likely to overshoot without policy action. "The inflation report implied quite strongly that they (BoE) will have to raise rates virtually straight away...Given that there is no one to stop them now," said Francis Breedon, senior foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers.
At midday in Europe, sterling stood at 2.7913/18 marks against 2.7808/13 in late Europe on Thursday, and some seven pfennigs up from a seven-week low at 2.7240 marks on Monday.
Against the dollar, sterling was trading at $1.6399/09 against $1.6384/94 and up over two cents from lows of $1.6154 hit on Monday.
"Sterling is a very wild currency. It can swing violently - still," said Ian Amstad, economist at Bankers Trust.
While sterling rocketed this week on a big fall in jobless figures, its blistering rally was not interrupted by softer than expected inflation and average earnings data, said analysts.
Analysts said this is because the weaker-than-forecast price and earnings data was unlikely to change the Bank of England's stance on the need for higher rates longer-term.

Britain's headline rate of inflation in April fell to 2.4 percent from 2.6 percent, while the underlying rate slid to 2.5 percent -- hitting the government's target -- from 2.7 percent. Underlying earnings rose 4.5 percent against a 5.0 percent forecast.
April unemployment, however, slid by 59,400 to 1.65 million, its lowest since August 1990, and highlighted the BoE's quest for higher rates.
"Even though we had good inflation numbers, it is probably not enough to turn them (BoE) around from their general position," said Lehman's Breedon.

Analysts say the only thing that could temper the possibility of even higher rates now is a tightening in fiscal policy, which could be announced when Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown delivers his first Budget, which could be as early as early June.
"Crucial is the fiscal stance. It they (government) don't do anything on fiscal policy, then rates are going up and up - peaking around 8.0 percent or above," said Breedon.

But because of sterling's strength in recent months, (it has soared from lows of 2.5769 marks in January, which has badly bruised exporters), fiscal tightening is seen as an attractive alternative, said analysts.
"Sterling will remain supported by views of higher rates, and that is unlikely to change until we have seen Mr Brown's budget," said CIBC's Coleman.
Failing this, analysts say speculation the pound could eventually re-join the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) will help.
Sterling crumbled some four pfennigs last week after a report by Bridge news, swiftly denied by the Treasury, said Britain planned to rejoin the EU's ERM at a central rate of 2.50 marks in 2001.

"Markets will be wary of taking it (sterling) up because the level it is at now is clearly too high for ERM entry. And even if we are in the second-tier of EMU it begs the question of when we have to participate in the ERM," said Bankers Trust's Amstad.

Sterling left the ERM in September 1992 after the government found it impossible to keep the currency near the then 2.95 central rate. The system was designed as a precursor to a single European currency. --London newsroom +4471 542 6701
